content: Peptic ulcer disease is a condition characterized by the development of ulcers in the lining of the stomach or the duodenum, primarily due to an imbalance between the aggressive factors in gastric juice and the defensive mechanisms of the gastric mucosa. The pathophysiology of this disease is mediated by two major factors that compromise mucosal resistance: infection with Helicobacter pylori and the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Helicobacter pylori is a gram-negative, spiral-shaped, urease-positive bacterium with high motility due to its flagella. Upon entering the stomach, it exhibits ureaseand bicarbonate-mediated chemotactic motility, allowing it to migrate toward the mucus layer. Its spiral morphology and flagellar motility facilitate penetration into the viscous mucus layer, where the pH is more neutral, enabling the bacterium to thrive. H. pylori produces virulence factors such as CagA and VacA, which activate interleukin-8 (IL-8), leading to inflammation of the gastric mucosa. Additionally, the bacterium secretes enzymes like urease, phospholipases, alcohol dehydrogenase, and catalase, which generate toxic metabolites and cause damage to the host gastric mucosa. NSAIDs contribute to peptic ulcer disease by inhibiting the production of systemic prostaglandins, which are essential for maintaining the integrity of the gastric mucosa. This inhibition leads to a higher prevalence of ulcers in the stomach compared to the duodenum. Other contributing factors include smoking, which reduces prostaglandin production in the fundic and antral regions of the stomach, causes bile acid reflux, and alters blood flow, leading to ischemia. In the case of duodenal ulcers, abnormalities in acid secretion are observed, such as increased basal acid output, heightened acid response to gastrin-releasing peptide (GRP), and decreased bicarbonate secretion. These changes result in gastric metaplasia-induced duodenitis, increasing the risk of acid damage and ulcer formation. Conversely, gastric ulcers are associated with reduced acid secretion and a decrease in parietal cell volume, predisposing the mucosa to ulcer development. Genetic factors also play a role in the pathogenesis of peptic ulcer disease. The CagA gene, present in certain H. pylori strains, encodes an immunodominant antigen linked to peptic ulcer disease. In duodenal ulcers, specific HLA-DQA1 genotypes, such as DQA10301, are more common in H. pylori-positive individuals, while DQA10102 alleles are more frequent in H. pylori-negative cases. Peptic ulcer disease is associated with several conditions, including gastric cancer, gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). H. pylori infection in duodenal ulcers can lead to gastric metaplasia and atrophy, increasing the risk of gastric cancer. Similarly, H. pylori infection is linked to the development of MALT lymphoma. In ITP, eradication therapy for H. pylori is recommended, as patients with peptic ulcer disease have an increased risk of developing this condition. Gross pathology of peptic ulcer disease involves macroscopic findings such as ulcers, which are characteristic of the disease. These findings are diagnostically significant and are often observed during surgical specimen processing or autopsy. Microscopic pathology, on the other hand, examines the disease process at the cellular level, revealing histopathological characteristics that are essential for diagnosis.
